newsitem.title: USA: Police scandal hits Giuliani in election year.
newsitem.headline: Police scandal hits Giuliani in election year.

text.p: Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, embroiled in a scandal over alleged police brutality in the middle of his re-election campaign, Friday defended the department whose crime-fighting success will probably secure him a second term.

Only two weeks after Giuliani and the police were bathed in glory when officers foiled a plot to blow up a city subway station, the mayor was forced to clean out a Brooklyn precinct over charges two officers sexually tortured a man in custody.

"He's got to be careful about what he says about the police," Columbia University politics professor Robert Shapiro said of the campaign. "The most potentially damaging thing is the reported comment by one of the officers that Dinkins is out and now Giuliani is in."

The Haitian man who has accused officers of assaulting him in a precinct house bathroom with a toilet plunger early Saturday said one of his attackers told him, "This is Giuliani time, not Dinkins time."

The reference to Giuliani's predecessor David Dinkins, the city's first black mayor, reverberated in black and Hispanic communities, where people have accused police of being more abusive in their duties during the past three years.

There were a spate of fatal shootings of minorities by police in 1996, including a unarmed Navy veteran shot in the back on a Bronx subway platorm, a unarmed 15-year-old shot dead in the back of a car and an unarmed man shot 18 times while sitting in a parked car.
But Giuliani sought to separate the alleged attack at the 70th precinct in Brooklyn from other allegations and defended the record of the country's largest police department.

"I believe that this is a situation in which the reputations of police officers will unfairly be affected," Giuliani said Friday on his "Live from City Hall" WABC Radio call-in program. "Prejudice means taking isolated facts, which may be true or untrue, and spreading that out into a gross, irrational over-generalization."
Giuliani said his analysis could be applied to racism, anti-Semitism or someone believing that all Italian-Americans had connections to Mafia crime families.

"They take the activities of some police officers which bear no resemblance at all to the activities of all police officers and then just cast group blame and will never defend police officers even when they're correct," Giuliani stated.
The Republican mayor's Democratic opponents in the November election are trailing in polls showing voters approve of declines in crime to the lowest levels in a generation.

Security guard Abner Louima, 30, told investigators he was arrested in a late-night brawl outside a nightclub, pushed to the ground, handcuffed, kicked and beaten. The immigrant from Haiti said he was taken to the stationhouse, where a toilet plunger handle was inserted into his rectum. He said the officers also shoved it into his mouth and smashed his teeth.
Louima was in critical but stable condition after surgery for a pierced rectum and torn bladder. He also suffered a fractured jaw and doctors say he needs more surgery.
Investigators said Friday that the key piece of evidence in the case, a toilet plunger, was missing.

Giuliani and Police Commissioner Howard Safir shook up the 70th precinct from top to bottom Wednesday, reassigning the top two officers and suspending or modifying the assignments of 10 other officers.
"I can smell something before I can see it or figure it out, I smell a cover up," Democratic Party mayoral candidate Rev. Al Sharpton said.

The only officer arrested so far was arraigned Thursday on sexual abuse and assault charges. Officials said four other officers may be involved and appealed to police to break the so-called blue wall of silence on the affair.
